meta.title: Distributed Job Scheduler
meta.summary: Run one-off and cron jobs for many tenants on time, at least once, with leases to catch dead workers, retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue.

functional: Submit one-off jobs (run now or at a given time) and recurring jobs (cron expression plus time zone) through an API
Each job calls an HTTP endpoint with its own timeout, retry policy and priority (high or standard)
Pause, resume and cancel jobs, and trigger a recurring job by hand
See each job's next run, its current state and every attempt from the last 30 days
Failed runs retry with exponential backoff; runs that use up their attempts go to a dead-letter queue for inspection and replay
Per-tenant limits on runs in flight at once
nonFunctional: A run starts within 10 s of its due time (p99), including at the top of the hour
At-least-once execution: an accepted run is never silently skipped. Duplicates are possible, so job targets must be idempotent
A run on a crashed worker is detected and rescheduled within about a minute
Two scheduler instances never dispatch the same due run
One busy tenant cannot delay other tenants' jobs
Survives the loss of one availability zone

scale.label: Top-of-hour spike
scale.value: Up to 200k runs due at :00, spread over 60 s by jitter (about 3.3k / s)

scale.label: Run history
scale.value: 30 days kept: about 1B attempt records, 500 GB

slos.name: Runs start on time
slos.sli: Runs whose start time (worker claim) minus due time is under the threshold, divided by all runs, excluding runs held back by their own tenant's quota

slos.name: Job API availability
slos.sli: Job API requests that do not return 5xx, divided by all requests, measured at the load balancer

slos.name: Dead workers caught quickly
slos.sli: Expired leases rescheduled within the threshold of lease_until, divided by all expired leases, measured from the runs table by the sweep

slos.name: No lost runs
slos.sli: Runs due more than 1 hour ago that reached a final state (succeeded, dead or cancelled), divided by all runs due more than 1 hour ago

alerts.when: Runs starting more than 10 s late burning the error budget 14 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes (a slow burn, 6 times over 6 hours, opens a ticket)
alerts.why: Jobs are firing late for many tenants, which is the main promise of a scheduler.

alerts.when: Job API 5xx burning the error budget 14 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes (a slow burn, 6 times over 6 hours, opens a ticket)
alerts.why: Tenants cannot create, cancel or inspect jobs.

alerts.when: Any run more than 15 minutes past due and still SCHEDULED or ENQUEUED, not held by a tenant quota, for 10 minutes
alerts.why: A run that nobody is going to pick up is a silently skipped job, the one failure the design promises never happens.

alerts.when: RUNNING rows with lease_until more than 2 minutes in the past for 5 minutes
alerts.why: The sweep has stopped, so runs on dead workers are never retried and their tenants' slots stay taken.

alerts.when: Oldest message in the standard queue above 60 s for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Workers are short of capacity. Scale-out should have handled it; find out why it did not before it turns into lag.

alerts.when: Lease expirations above 1% of runs for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Workers are dying mid-run (out of memory, bad deploys, ungraceful scale-in) or heartbeats are failing. Every expiry is a retry and a possible duplicate.

alerts.when: More than 500 dead-lettered runs in an hour, or more than 50 for one tenant
alerts.why: A target is broken or a tenant deployed a bug. Someone should look and tell the tenant before replaying.

alerts.when: Dispatch query p99 above 250 ms for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Usually index bloat or vacuum falling behind on the runs table. It comes before start lag.

alerts.when: Jobs DB failover happened, or primary CPU above 75% for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Dispatch, claims and heartbeats all write to one primary; saturation shows up as start lag next.

signals.name: Due backlog
signals.why: SCHEDULED runs whose due time has passed. Growing means dispatch cannot keep up.

signals.name: Start lag by priority
signals.why: Claim time minus due time: the number tenants actually feel.

signals.name: Lease expirations and fenced writes
signals.why: Fenced writes count late results from zombie workers that the attempt check rejected.

signals.name: Runs deferred by tenant quota
signals.why: Shows which tenants are at their limit, so their lateness is not mistaken for a platform problem.

signals.name: Dead tuples on the runs table
signals.why: Every state change rewrites a row. If vacuum falls behind, the due-runs index bloats and dispatch slows.

signals.name: Age of the oldest message
signals.why: Separates slow dispatch (backlog in the database) from too few workers (backlog in the queue).

steps: Find where the backlog sits: due runs piling up in the database means dispatch is slow, an old queue message means workers are short.
If dispatch is slow, check dispatch query latency, lock waits and dead tuples on the runs table, and that all scheduler instances are running.
If workers are short, check worker count against queue age and whether scale-out is reacting fast enough before the top of the hour.
Break lag down by tenant: if one tenant is late because it is at its quota, that is the quota working, not an outage.

debug.symptom: A tenant says a job ran twice
steps: Look up the run id in the history: two attempts with different attempt numbers means a lease expired and the run was retried.
Check the first worker's heartbeats and logs around the expiry: a crash, a long GC pause or a network partition.
Compare lease length with the heartbeat interval; leases should survive at least two missed heartbeats.
Check that the target honors the Idempotency-Key header. Duplicates are part of the contract, so the fix may be on their side.

nodes.label: Tenant Services
nodes.description: Tenant backends and the web console calling the Job API

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the API hostname at the load balancer, which has the WAF attached

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Attached to the load balancer: managed rule sets, per-tenant and per-IP rate rules, bot control on the console

nodes.label: Load Balancer (L7)
nodes.description: TLS termination and HTTP routing to the Job API

nodes.label: Job API
nodes.description: Validates jobs and cron expressions, enforces tenant limits, serves status and history

nodes.label: Jobs DB
nodes.description: Source of truth: job definitions, tenant limits and one row per active run with state, due time, attempt and lease. Survives a zone loss (Aurora keeps 6 storage copies across 3 zones; Cloud SQL HA keeps a synchronous standby in another zone); a failover pauses dispatch for under a minute or so, which shows up as start lag, not lost runs

nodes.label: Scheduler
nodes.description: Every second claims due runs with SKIP LOCKED and enqueues them; also sweeps expired leases and owns the retry policy

nodes.label: Dead-letter Queue
nodes.description: Notification copy of runs whose row is DEAD in the Jobs DB; operator tooling and tenant alerts consume it. Replay goes through the Job API, which moves the DEAD row back to SCHEDULED

nodes.label: Workers
nodes.description: Claim a run with a lease, heartbeat while it runs, call the target, record the result. Each task holds hundreds of target calls at once (40k in flight at peak), and reaches the internet through NAT with fixed egress IPs

nodes.label: Run History
nodes.description: One record per attempt, keyed by job id and time, expired after 30 days

nodes.label: Tenant Endpoints
nodes.description: The HTTP endpoints jobs call; expected to honor an idempotency key

flows.title: Submit a recurring job
flows.summary: Validate the cron expression, then write the job and its first run in one transaction. Nothing is scheduled in memory, so any scheduler instance can pick it up.

steps.label: resolve jobs.example.com
steps.detail: The tenant's service finds the load balancer by name, so its addresses can change without client updates.

steps.label: POST /v1/jobs
steps.detail: The idempotency key makes a retried submit return the same job instead of creating a second one that would run every night as well.

steps.label: inspect, then forward
steps.detail: Managed rule sets, per-tenant and per-IP rate rules and bot control on the console stop abuse before it reaches the API, which still enforces each tenant's own limits.

steps.label: forward to any API instance
steps.detail: The API is stateless, so any instance in any zone can take the request.

steps.label: parse cron, compute first run
steps.detail: The next fire time is computed in the job's own time zone, so 02:00 New York stays 02:00 across daylight saving changes. A stable offset of hash(job_id) mod 60 s spreads jobs that all say 02:00 across a minute.

steps.label: INSERT job + first run
steps.detail: The job and its first run row are written in one transaction, so a job can never exist without a next run to fire. The run id is derived from the job and its scheduled time, and a unique constraint stops the same occurrence being created twice.

steps.label: COMMIT ok
steps.detail: Committed durably across zones (Aurora's quorum storage, or Cloud SQL's synchronous standby), so the job survives a zone failure.

flows.title: A due job is dispatched and run
flows.summary: A scheduler claims due rows with SKIP LOCKED, checks the tenant quota and enqueues them; a worker claims the run with a lease, heartbeats while it calls the target, then records the result.

steps.label: tick (every 1 s)
steps.detail: All three scheduler instances run this loop at the same time. There is no leader: the database lock in the next step decides who gets which rows. An instance whose batch comes back full loops again at once instead of waiting for the next tick: at the top of the hour about 3.3k runs/s come due, more than 500 rows per second per instance would cover.

steps.label: SELECT due FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
steps.detail: SKIP LOCKED makes each instance take a different batch of due rows instead of waiting on or double-taking the same ones. A partial index on due_at covering only SCHEDULED rows keeps this fast however many finished runs exist. Due times are compared with the database clock, so skew between scheduler hosts does not matter.
steps.payload:
BEGIN;
SELECT run_id, job_id, tenant_id, priority
FROM runs
WHERE state = 'SCHEDULED' AND due_at <= now()
ORDER BY priority, due_at
LIMIT 500
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

steps.label: count in-flight runs per tenant
steps.detail: Fairness is enforced before anything reaches the shared queue. An index on (tenant_id, state) makes this a cheap count for the tenants in the batch. Two schedulers counting at once can overshoot a limit by a few runs, which is fine for fairness; a strict limit would need a counter row updated in the same transaction.
steps.payload:
SELECT r.tenant_id, count(*) AS in_flight, t.max_in_flight
FROM runs r JOIN tenants t USING (tenant_id)
WHERE r.tenant_id = ANY($batch_tenants) AND r.state IN ('ENQUEUED', 'RUNNING')
GROUP BY r.tenant_id, t.max_in_flight;

steps.label: t_acme: 47 of 50 in flight, admit 3
steps.detail: Runs over a tenant's limit are not enqueued. Their due_at is pushed back a few seconds, so they wait in the database and never fill the shared queue ahead of other tenants.

steps.label: SendMessageBatch (10 per call)
steps.detail: Priority picks the queue. The message carries only the run id and a trace context; the database row stays the source of truth.

steps.label: mark ENQUEUED, insert next run, COMMIT
steps.detail: Messages are sent while the rows are still locked, then the transaction commits. A crash in between leaves the rows SCHEDULED to be sent again: a duplicate message, never a lost run. For cron jobs the next occurrence is inserted now, so the schedule continues even if this run is slow or fails.

steps.label: receive (visibility timeout 5 min)
steps.detail: Workers long-poll the high-priority queue more often than the standard one (for example 3 to 1), so urgent runs go first without starving the rest.

steps.label: UPDATE ... SET state = 'RUNNING' RETURNING attempt
steps.detail: A conditional update claims the run: only one worker can move it out of ENQUEUED, so a duplicate message finds 0 rows and is dropped. The lease says how long the claim lasts without a heartbeat. The new attempt number doubles as a fencing token. A RUNNING row also counts toward its tenant's in-flight limit until it finishes.
steps.payload:
UPDATE runs
SET state = 'RUNNING', attempt = attempt + 1, worker_id = 'w-17',
    started_at = now(), lease_until = now() + interval '60 seconds'
WHERE run_id = 'r_8c2_20261111T0700Z'
  AND state IN ('SCHEDULED', 'ENQUEUED') AND due_at <= now()
RETURNING attempt, target, timeout_s;

steps.label: DeleteMessage
steps.detail: Once the row is claimed, the lease in the database protects the run, so the message is deleted. If the worker had died before claiming, the message would reappear after the visibility timeout and another worker would take it.

steps.label: POST /hooks/export
steps.detail: Execution is at least once, so this call may be a repeat of an earlier attempt. The run id is sent as an idempotency key and the target uses it to skip work it already did. The request is signed with a key from the secrets manager so the tenant can verify it came from the scheduler, and the trace context lets a tenant line up our attempt with their own logs.
steps.payload:
POST /hooks/export
Idempotency-Key: r_8c2_20261111T0700Z
X-Job-Attempt: 1
X-Signature: t=1762844413,v1=5d1e...
traceparent: 00-9f2c4d1a7be04c3e8d55a1f0e6b2c7d9-6c8e0a2b4d6f8a1c-01

{ "job_id": "j_8c2", "scheduled_for": "2026-11-11T07:00:00Z" }

steps.label: heartbeat every 20 s: extend lease
steps.detail: While the call runs, the worker pushes lease_until forward. A 60 s lease with 20 s heartbeats tolerates two missed beats. If the update matches 0 rows, the worker has lost its lease and abandons the run.
steps.payload:
UPDATE runs SET lease_until = now() + interval '60 seconds'
WHERE run_id = 'r_8c2_20261111T0700Z' AND attempt = 1 AND state = 'RUNNING';

steps.label: SET state = 'SUCCEEDED' WHERE attempt = 1
steps.detail: The attempt check fences the write: if this worker's lease had expired and a retry had started, its late result would match 0 rows and be discarded instead of overwriting the newer attempt.
steps.payload:
UPDATE runs SET state = 'SUCCEEDED', finished_at = now()
WHERE run_id = 'r_8c2_20261111T0700Z' AND attempt = 1 AND state = 'RUNNING';

steps.label: append attempt record
steps.detail: Attempt details go to a store built for a billion append-only records, keeping the hot runs table small. Finished run rows are deleted from the database later by the scheduler's cleanup pass, once their record is in history.

flows.title: Worker dies mid-job: lease expires, retries, dead-letter
flows.summary: No one reports a dead worker. The scheduler notices the lease ran out, reschedules with backoff, and after the last allowed attempt moves the run to the dead-letter queue.

steps.label: receive r_41a (hourly reconcile)
steps.detail: A high-priority job for tenant t_globex, allowed 5 attempts.

steps.label: POST /hooks/reconcile
steps.detail: The target starts the work. Whether it finishes is unknown to the scheduler from here on.

steps.label: host lost: heartbeats stop
steps.detail: Nothing sends a failure message: the process is gone, or merely frozen by a long GC pause or a network partition. The only evidence is that lease_until stops moving forward.

steps.label: sweep tick (every 5 s)
steps.detail: The same scheduler instances that dispatch also sweep, again sharing the work through SKIP LOCKED.

steps.label: SELECT expired leases + stale ENQUEUED
steps.detail: Leases are judged by the database clock, so a scheduler with a skewed clock cannot expire a healthy run early. The same sweep resets runs stuck in ENQUEUED for 10 minutes (a lost or expired message) back to SCHEDULED, which is what makes "never silently skipped" hold; a duplicate message is harmless because the claim is conditional.
steps.payload:
SELECT run_id, tenant_id, state, attempt, retry
FROM runs
WHERE (state = 'RUNNING' AND lease_until < now())
   OR (state = 'ENQUEUED' AND enqueued_at < now() - interval '10 minutes')
LIMIT 500
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

steps.label: r_41a, attempt 1 of 5, expired 3 s ago
SCHEDULED, due in 30 s + jitter
steps.detail: The scheduler owns the retry policy for every kind of failure. The delay doubles each attempt (30 s, 60 s, 120 s, 240 s, capped at 1 h) plus up to 20% random jitter, so many failed runs do not all retry in the same second. Leaving RUNNING also frees the tenant's in-flight slot. If the old worker was only paused and wakes up, its next heartbeat or result fails the attempt check and it stops.

steps.label: attempt 5 failed: SET state = 'DEAD'
steps.detail: Attempts 2 to 5 travel the normal dispatch path over the next 8 minutes or so, and each one fails because the target keeps returning 500. When the retry pass sees attempt 5 fail it stops retrying, because the job's max_attempts is reached.

steps.label: publish dead run
steps.detail: Published while the row is still locked, then the transaction commits, as in dispatch: a crash in between dead-letters the run again, so the queue may hold a duplicate but never misses one. The run is parked, not dropped: an alert fires, the tenant sees it as dead in the console, and it can be replayed once the target is fixed. The 10:00 occurrence of this hourly job was already inserted at dispatch, so the schedule carries on.

flows.title: Check a job's status and history
flows.summary: Current state comes from the jobs database; past attempts come from the history store.

steps.label: GET /v1/jobs/j_8c2/runs?limit=20
steps.detail: The tenant's console asks for the job, its next run and its recent attempts.

steps.label: SELECT job and its open runs
steps.detail: Only the database knows what is happening right now: the next due time and any run that is queued or running, with its attempt and lease.

steps.label: Query pk = j_8c2, newest first, 20
steps.detail: History is keyed by job id and time, so the latest attempts for one job are a single range read, however many jobs the tenant has.

notes.text: Exactly-once execution is not achievable in general: a worker can finish the work and die before recording it, and nobody can tell that apart from dying before the work. The design picks at-least-once with an idempotency key per run. Jobs where a duplicate is worse than a miss can opt into at-most-once: mark the run started before calling and never retry it.

Three ways to stop two schedulers taking the same run: one elected leader (simple, but one instance does all the work and failover pauses dispatch), partitions owned through leases (scales out, but rebalancing is real work), or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on one database (no coordination at all, limited by that database). SKIP LOCKED is enough at this scale; partition ownership is the next step.

If dispatch stops for 20 minutes, due runs simply wait in the database and are overdue on recovery. Each job's misfire policy decides what happens: run once (the default, since only the next occurrence exists) or skip if more than a grace period late. One-off jobs always run. Cron times use the job's time zone: a 02:30 run is skipped on the spring-forward night unless the policy moves it, and a 01:30 run must not fire twice in autumn.

Every run causes several writes (dispatch, claim, heartbeats, result): about 20k row writes per second at the top-of-hour peak. Keep the runs table small by having the scheduler delete finished rows once they are in history, give the due-runs index a partial condition on state, and tune autovacuum for heavy churn. Beyond one primary, shard runs by hash(job_id) and give each scheduler a set of shards.

Most cron jobs say minute 0, which creates a thundering herd at the top of the hour. A stable per-job jitter spreads them over a minute, workers scale out on queue age and a few minutes before the hour, and per-tenant quotas keep one tenant's 50k hourly jobs from filling the queues.

Workers call URLs that tenants choose, which is a server-side request forgery risk. Resolve the hostname and refuse private, link-local and metadata addresses, sign every request with a key held in a secrets manager (Secrets Manager or Secret Manager) and rotated, and send traffic through NAT with fixed egress IPs that tenants can allowlist. Inbound, the WAF in front of the load balancer filters abuse before the API checks the tenant token.

questions.q: Can you guarantee that each job runs exactly once?
questions.a: Not in general: a worker can complete the work and crash before recording success, and the system cannot tell that from a crash before the work, so it must either retry (risking a duplicate) or not (risking a miss). The design chooses at-least-once and sends the run id as an idempotency key, so a target that records processed keys gets effectively-once results. Fencing writes by attempt number also stops a stale worker from overwriting a newer attempt's outcome.

questions.q: You run three scheduler instances for availability. How do you stop two of them dispatching the same run?
questions.a: Each instance claims due rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction, so rows locked by one instance are skipped by the others rather than shared. Alternatives are a single leader chosen by a lease in etcd or ZooKeeper, which pauses dispatch during failover, or partitioning runs and leasing partitions to instances, which scales past one database. A unique constraint on (job_id, scheduled_for) stops the next occurrence of a cron job being created twice.

questions.q: A worker dies halfway through a job. How does the system notice, and what stops the old worker from writing a result later if it was only paused?
questions.a: The claim gives the worker a 60 s lease that it extends with a heartbeat every 20 s; a sweep in the scheduler finds RUNNING rows whose lease has passed and reschedules them with backoff. The attempt number set at claim is a fencing token: every heartbeat and result write includes it, so a worker that wakes up after a GC pause matches 0 rows, learns it lost the lease and stops. The lease length is a trade-off between detecting crashes quickly and falsely expiring slow but healthy workers.

questions.q: 200,000 jobs are due at exactly midnight. How do you avoid a thundering herd?
questions.a: Give each job a stable jitter offset, such as hash(job_id) mod 60 s, so they spread over a minute while each job still fires at the same moment every day. Scale workers ahead of known peaks rather than waiting for the queue to grow, and keep dispatch batched (500 rows per query, 10 messages per send). Tenant quotas stop any single tenant's burst from taking the whole capacity.

questions.q: The schedulers were down for 20 minutes. What happens to the runs that came due during the outage?
questions.a: They are not lost, because due runs are rows in the database rather than timers in memory; when dispatch resumes they are simply overdue and get picked up oldest first. A per-job misfire policy then decides: run once and compute the next time from now, or skip runs more than a grace period late, for jobs like a report that is useless after the fact. Catching up every missed occurrence is rarely wanted, and the scheduler compares due times with the database clock so host clock skew cannot cause early or missed runs.

questions.q: One tenant submits a million jobs at once. How do you keep everyone else's jobs on time?
questions.a: The scheduler counts each tenant's queued and running runs before enqueuing, and runs over the tenant's limit stay in the database with a slightly later due time instead of filling the shared queue. The API also rate-limits submissions and caps active jobs per tenant. Priority queues polled in a weighted ratio protect urgent work, and the start-lag SLO excludes runs held by their own tenant's quota so throttling a noisy tenant does not look like an outage.
